posts.author: LaCipolla
posts.body:
My game is out in just under a week, my head is spinning with a lot of annoying publicity… So it should be the perfect time to take a step back.
(This was originally a dev blog post for my game, but I think it is also decidedly more than that. ^^ If you'd prefer to read it in German, you'll find it
here
.)
Remembering 200X​
My first impression of RPG Maker was probably
Ente die Ente
or “Duck the Duck” – capturing the tone of the game perfectly! We were at a friend’s place, and even though, in that moment, the vast world of video game development was slowly opening up before me, I mainly remember cartoon animals made with MS Paint and an antagonist named Atze Hutler. I also learned of
Vampires Dawn
that day, with its deeply adolescent fondness for fountains of blood and a completely ridiculous excess of exclamation marks. If a game looked actually good back then, though, the resources were DEFINITELY ripped from
Secret of Mana
or some other jrpg. (Most developers had no clue!) Even the trendy youth mag
Bravo
‘s spin-off
Screenfun
didn’t give a damn about any of that when they burned RPG Maker games with exactly those quality standards onto their print run of 100,000 cover CDs.
Welcome to the German RPG Maker scene of the early 2000s!
Back then, I didn’t actually play all that much. I just wanted to make games, but unfortunately I was also 15 ing years old. And although I have tremendous respect for the people who, at 15, took on massive projects (“Final Fantasy, but as an MMO!!”) – and then actually SAW THEM THROUGH
in
some
form
or another – I definitely was NOT one of those people. What I was able to do, however, was posting, on the community forums! No matter what they were named at a certain point (from
RPG-Ring
to
Multimediaxis
), which subforums merged or split off in a rage, whoever was currently muddling forum politics and personal relationship drama … These message boards were always there. Especially the creative parts! Community meetups like the NATO (please don’t ask) or the still ongoing
BMT
were social trials by fire that probably saved me single-handedly from the weirdest excesses of being a real ing nerd. In fact, most of my friends today – and my partner! – hail from these forums as well. You know who you are! <3
So much about me, yada yada. BUT …
RPG Maker is just REALLY cool!​
Right? I know, my community has spent 25 years venting in walls of text, sprawling quote battles, and 100% personal flame wars about the engine and its weaknesses … But the advantages are far too often taken for granted. Not today! ;D
RPG Maker is a chill middle ground.
Of course there are more common engines, and more powerful ones, but RPG Maker also works for beginners with zero background knowledge, with just a few simple YouTube tutorials … and STILL provides ways to dive deeper into all the technical underpinnings. I’d even say it motivates you to do so, precisely at the points where it is limited for the sake of simplicity. (But you can also just… NOT do that, which is at least as valuable!)
Role-playing games are perfectly suited for teenage nerds.
RPGs are fantasies, they literally let us slip into another role, they’re practically THE genre for escapism – but of course also for utopia and dystopia, for symbolism and allegory, ultimately for exploring yourself. If someone wants to express themselves through video games? RPGs! o/
RPG Maker offers access to a complex genre.
RPGs, however, are also HARD, multidisciplinary, ideally with epic music, deep writing, beautiful art design, and so on and so forth … And RPG Maker delivers all of that in one cohesive package. Experienced developers might wrinkle their noses when they detect even a smidge of the standard resources, but getting cool anime-style portraits and ready-made sound effects delivered in a way that actually fits together? That’s PRICELESS!
It’s just so… free!
I don’t necessarily mean the “free” resources that were oh so cheerfully ripped from popular jrpgs back then … but maybe I do! On the more legal side, I can find virtually endless games without spending a cent, and free resources for PRACTICALLY EVERYTHING! But I also love that I can play a Dragon Ball fangame from Brazil, or a Japanese horror game that makes me question the developer’s mental health, or visual novels with or without (but mostly with) a lot of porn. And if I want to advertise my game, I can use RPG Maker’s fonts, symbols, and even music. None of that is a given.
RPG Maker has FLAIR.
Sure, people love to say “you should just use Engine XY instead!” … but dear people? RPG Maker is a BRAND, and for once (!), I mean that in a positive sense. The cohesive overall package has a part in that, but perhaps even more important is the history, the entirety of projects and experiences attached to it, precisely because RPG Maker is such a specific thing. On the one hand, we have truly big, impressive games, often with artistic ambitions (Ever pedaled full speed off a cliff in
LISA
? Ever groaned at a pop culture joke in
To the Moon
?), and on the other hand, we have a huge amount of trash … intensely PERSONAL trash! And together with the community, all of that creates real flair. <3
When I look at these two paragraphs again, I 100% understand why RPG Maker brought so many teenagers together, back then. It certainly helped that it used to be, uh, “free”, of course
*
cough*, and that today you can get older versions dirt cheap – especially for teenagers, and ESPECIALLY in regions that are less privileged and less equipped with modern consoles. Democratic game development for everyone!
So what now?​
Not to ruin the mood, but I’m afraid
Minecraft
– and especially
Roblox
! – have taken RPG Maker’s place, at least for most teenagers. And aside from the faceless malevolent mega-corporations behind them, that might not even be such a bad thing …? =_=’ I still recommend RPG Maker though!
Obviously, I also dusted off the engine a few years ago. That was insanely nostalgic, with some skills coming back instantly, but it was also quite a wild learning experience, being in my late 30s with a somewhat functional sense of myself and what I can (not) do… So yeah, I actually managed to finish a few things, and
Monster Girl Therapy
releases on March 10! ;D But aside from said publicity stuff, I also just found it incredibly cool to really “dive in” again, to see that a lot has changed (often for the better!) and to see that there’s still SO MUCH going on here. In that sense, dear RPG Maker and dear RPG Maker people: Thanks a lot, I love you very much! <3
Feel free to share your own memories, too!

posts.author: fizzly
posts.body: I discovered RPG Maker completely by accident. It started with a game (actually, it was weak and probably unbeatable, but I really liked the graphics and music at the time – it was all RTP!) called Mage's Quest. I found it on a magazine disc. In the game's catalog, I found RTP chipsets, and I was so eager to build my own game with them that I glued the tiles together in...MS Paint xD I had no idea RPG Maker existed or that this game was being made with it. After a few years, I found other similar games and was puzzled by the recurring graphics. In the catalog of one of them, I found credits that said the game was made using RPG Maker 2000. That was the beginning of my love affair...

posts.author: Banana_Duck
posts.body:
There was a time I was really interested in Final Fantasy, the late 2000s, I was a preteen then, I grabbed vanilla VX because it was the newest version at the time (VX Ace wasn't released yet), and me and my sis (and later my little brother too, he's using XP) made crappy fanfics with it.
I was even active on French forums back then, I even talked about my really crappy comedy game that had about fifty one-note playable characters, most of them with designs from the RTP, a self-insert narrator, references everywhere, stolen music, and the worst humor ever. Nobody liked it, not even my sister.
Fast-forward to today, and I'm spending hundreds of hours planning my current game on VX Ace, which is an amalgamation of the stuff I learned from watching thousands of video essays and reading countless forum posts and wikis. And so far, it sucks much, much less than any of my previous attempts.

posts.author: Iron_Brew
posts.body:
I've always wanted to make video games. The first time I played a game I thought "this is the best thing I've ever seen and I want to make this for other people."
My game development journey started at 8 years old with Klik 'N' Play, which my dad picked up on a whim in a charity shop. I'll never forget downloading the demo for the "sequel" engine, Game Maker, on 56k - it was 10MB, which meant an hour sat staring at the download bar, praying nobody called the house. From there, I got onto Visual Basic and I'd take games in on floppy discs, and later, CDs - and give them out on the playground at school.
Then, as a teenager, I discovered RPG Maker. I got commissioned to do a couple of bits and pieces for local businesses - broadly making cutscenes for use in stylised commercials, or what have you. All the while I'd be learning, and using the visual scripting of the prior engines and knowledge I'd gained in creating loops and game design as a whole and taking them back to RPG Maker to prototype experimental little things. The engine was fantastic for getting everything you needed to prototype quickly, and then slam things into place, and the lack of overhead in terms of assets or technical nouse was a great shortcut if I wanted to get something off the ground quickly.
I made a couple of longer projects - one of which was a 25-hour game featuring EXTREMELY local jokes - and when I finished Uni (for an entirely different field) I could legitimately say "I have created a game in a collaborative environment, overseeing a team of contributors who had skills I didn't have and oversaw a release cycle". The game did OK, and had a ton of testers, and later, players - and that felt great.
When an opportunity came up at a local game studio, I applied, and parlayed that collaborative development experience into a hyper-entry-level job, where the kind of experience RPG Maker had helped me accrue played an invaluable part in my employability into that role.
I have now been a professional game developer for twelve years, moved cities, met people I love; my life has been inexorably changed for the better all because RPG Maker helped continue the legacy of those entry-level game engines. I've even gone to meet up with other RPG Maker creators on another continent.
I'll never stop advocating for this little engine.
Even though I'd never advise its use at scale at scale, even though it
definitely
sucks in myriad ways, and even though 99% of what's made with it is either terrible or unfinished; because without RPG Maker my life would have never become what it is. I fully attribute the dawn of my career to the early success I found with RPG Maker.
And I'm a
dummy
.
If RPG Maker can open doors for me, RPG Maker can do the same for you. All you gotta do, is do it.

posts.author: RCXGaming
posts.body:
My story with RPG Maker is a simple one: I played with XP back in 2005(-ish) back when I was a wee tot that didn't have money. I wanted to finish a project in the 30 day trial and basically scrambled to the finish knowing absolutely nothing about how the system worked or what scripts were or whatever. I still look back fondly on those days - probably even more so because I never saved the files to know for sure how bad the demo really was.
Ever since then, it was my tool of choice to work on something to spend an afternoon on. Around 2012, I started using it to make little recreations of the RP sessions with my friends.
I wasn't really part of any RPG Maker "scene" or even know about any RM games other than Yume Nikki and its unofficial sequel, I just kinda hung out in the back doing my own thing. It wasn't until 2016 where I finally started to branch out and look for resources to use in a game I wanted to make for real, not just for my friends.
I've upgraded from VX Ace to MV across those years, and frankly... as much as I loved Ace, I don't think I'll ever go back.
I stick to RM because for me, it's an easy way to bring my storytelling to life without having to spend hundreds of hours recreating the basics. It's frankly a thrill trying to think of ways to recreate mechanics from other games in RM, especially with how the Javascript-based makers allow you to do pretty much whatever you want.
I've made peace with the fact my time with RM might not last forever, especially if I get more ambitious, but it's like home to me.

posts.author: Indinera
posts.body:
Where to begin?
I've been with RM for 25 years of my life. Seen many eras, used many RM installments,
RM2K
for the
Laxius Power
trilogy,
RMXP
for the
Laxius Force
trilogy and the
Millennium
series (among many others), them
RMVX
and
VX Ace
for various collaborations notably with Gemelle Games (such as
Undefeated
or
The Tale of a Common Man
), then a bit of
MV
and now I'm using
MZ
and I've notably made
Laxius Soul
with it, launching the final trilogy of the series.
I created Aldorlea Games in 2009 to support my commercial venture (soon releasing third party games too) and enjoyed a healthy long-lasting following, and became a Steam publisher specializing solely in RM games in 2015 with many years of successful releases (over 75 games grossing 5 figures or more).
This little software changed my life irreversibly, probably for the best.
I was born poor in a very competitive country, so it wasn't going to be easy, and RPG Maker came along and gave me a profession, a career, plenty of free time, allowed me to see the world and to be available for people that mattered. It was also behind countless lovely encounters both IVL and IRL (but especially IRL). I wouldn't be with my wife without RPG Maker. I wouldn't be the person I'm now without it.
Even if it's not been easy and involved a lot of hard work and consistency, I cannot imagine a life without it.
RPG Maker allowed me to develop some of my main passions (like storytelling, game designing and to some lesser extent music) and share them to the world, and for that I'm eternally grateful to it.
